newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asia regional currencies, whither the crosses/trade.
newsitem.headline: Asia regional currencies, whither the crosses/trade.

text.p: Three weeks of turmoil on regional financial markets has seen the spotlight fall on Asian currencies' significant losses against the U.S. dollar, but falls have been uneven and resulted in a somewhat different picture on the crosses.

Analysts said on Wednesday that with the Asian regional trade generally in surplus with the United States, devaluing against the dollar can be seen as basically good news in terms of export competitiveness.
But the opposite is true of Japan with some deficits quite large and weakness against the yen could well cause economic problems in the near to medium term, they said.

"You have seen the most Japanese investment in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand and the yen crosses have changed fundamentally but by different magnitudes," said Kobus Van Der Wath, regional head of treasury economist at Standard Chartered in Singapore.
For example, Malaysian exports to Singapore made up 20.5 percent of the total last year, leading to a surplus with Singapore of nearly 14 billion ringgit.

There was also surplus with the U.S. of 5.3 billion ringgit, but with Japan there was a deficit of over 22 billion ringgit. Japan was Malaysia's largest trading partner with around 19 percent of total trade.

This kind of trade picture is fairly consistent in the Asian region and economists said the move against the yen is going to have an "J" curve effect. In other words things will get worse before they get better.

The "J" curve describes the reaction of the balance of trade following a devaluation. First a trade deficit deteriorates as import costs rise but further out it improves as volumes expand on the back of more competitive prices of exports due to the currency effect.
There will also be a "J" curve effect because of the devaluations against the dollar, but it will not be so pronounced as there are generally surpluses of exports over imports with the United States.

"Asian regional countries tend to import capital goods from Japan so the cost of investment goes up unless the Japanese exporter shaves prices," said Manu Bhaskaran, group head of research at SocGen-Crosby Securities in Singapore.
But because the falls against the yen have been of different magnitudes some countries will suffer more than others.

"The trade shortfalls with Japan are the reason we think current account deficits will not look too good. For example, Thailand will take a big hit with the recent improvement in the current account deficit stalling."

There is then the danger that a deterioration in the current account position feeds through into further selling of the currency. If a situation like this develops, it will simply prolong the agony for Asian regional currencies, analysts said.

Apart from the yen crosses, there have been some sizable moves elsewhere, the most important being ringgit/Singapore dollar which has dropped quite sharply, around two percent, as the ringgit fell more than the Singapore dollar during the recent crisis.
With over 20 percent of Malaysian exports going to Singapore, a rise in competitiveness is not unwelcome.

"Ringgit/Sing (Singapore dollar) bears watching and Malaysia, in terms of trade, has done quite well out of ringgit's decline on the Singapore dollar," said Chiang Yao Chye, economist at CIBC Wood Gundy in Singapore.
"As long as there is not another panic run on the ringgit again I would have thought this position is something they are quite comfortable with."
